title: THE NIGHT THAT DOES NOT ANSWER
text: Imagine that tomorrow, an observatory detects a signal that repeats from the direction of another star. The pattern looks deliberate. A second telescope checks. Then a third. The signal is still there. For a moment, humanity has a new question: who is speaking? Now return to tonight. We have no such confirmed announcement. Above us are stars, planets, radiation, and an enormous amount we have barely examined. What we do not have is verified evidence of another technological civilization. That gap is the heart of the Fermi paradox. If our galaxy has had so much time, and so many places where life might arise, where is everybody? But there is a trap inside that question. It can make us imagine that scientists have listened to the entire universe and heard nothing. They have not. Before we decide that the silence is frightening, comforting, or meaningful, we need to ask what silence actually means. This story begins with an empty chair at a radio telescope. It ends with a different way of looking at the sky.

title: A QUESTION, NOT A CONTRADICTION
text: The question is associated with physicist Enrico Fermi and a lunchtime conversation in nineteen fifty. The familiar phrase, where is everybody, became shorthand for a much wider argument developed by many people. We do not need to reconstruct every detail of that lunch to understand the problem. The universe seems to offer a great deal of time and opportunity. Some arguments suggest that a civilization capable of spreading between stars could become widely distributed within a fraction of the galaxy's age. Yet we do not observe an unmistakably inhabited galaxy. That sounds contradictory only if several assumptions are true. Technological life must arise often enough. It must survive. It must spread, or produce signals we can detect. And we must have searched in the right way. Change those assumptions, and the apparent contradiction changes too. The Fermi paradox is therefore not a measurement proving that aliens should be here. It is a confrontation between expectations and observations. Its value comes from making us unpack those expectations, one by one, instead of treating our first intuition as a law of nature.

title: THE SCALE OF THE ADDRESS
text: Start with our address. Earth circles one ordinary star in the Milky Way, a galaxy roughly a hundred thousand light-years across, with hundreds of billions of stars by common estimates. These are broad scale estimates, not a complete census. A light-year is a distance: the distance light travels in a year. When we look across the galaxy, we are not seeing one simultaneous present. We are receiving messages from different moments in the past. The Moon is nearby enough that a radio exchange involves seconds. A conversation with a star system ten light-years away would involve at least twenty years between sending a question and receiving an immediate reply. A technological civilization could be alive right now in some meaningful shared frame and still be inaccessible to a real-time conversation. Distance is not a minor inconvenience added to the story. It shapes the story from the beginning. The night sky feels like one room with many lights. Physically, it is a vast landscape in which even the fastest possible news travels slowly compared with a human life.

title: PLANETS ARE COMMON; EARTHS ARE ANOTHER QUESTION
text: One part of the old mystery has changed dramatically. We now know that planets are common around other stars. Astronomers have confirmed thousands of exoplanets through methods such as transits and stellar motion. That is a statement about a growing catalog, not an exact total that will remain current forever. We have found a remarkable variety of systems: giant planets close to their stars, compact families of small worlds, and planets unlike anything in our own neighborhood. But a planet is not automatically a habitat. A world with Earth's approximate size is not automatically another Earth. A planet in a star's habitable zone has an orbit where surface liquid water might be possible under suitable conditions. The phrase does not certify oceans, breathable air, a stable climate, or life. Atmosphere, stellar activity, geological history, and many other conditions matter. Finding many planets enlarges the number of possible settings. It does not tell us how often the essential events actually happen inside those settings. Opportunity is a crucial ingredient, but opportunity and outcome are different quantities.

title: THE FIRST MISSING PROBABILITY
text: Suppose we found a world with an ocean, energy sources, and useful chemistry. How likely is it that life would begin there? We do not know. On Earth, life emerged early in the planet's history, but that observation is not a simple stopwatch revealing a universal rate. We have an incomplete early record, uncertainty about relevant conditions, and an observer problem: we necessarily find ourselves on a world where enough time remained for observers to appear. Laboratories have investigated important steps in prebiotic chemistry. No laboratory result yet gives us a reliable probability that a suitable planet will produce a living system over a given interval. Nor have we confirmed a second independent origin of life. If we found organisms elsewhere, we would need to ask whether they represent a separate origin or share ancestry through transported material. A genuinely independent example would change this discussion enormously. Until then, the leap from many habitable environments to many inhabited environments is still a leap. It may turn out to be a small one. We do not get to assume that it is.

title: A MICROBIAL GALAXY COULD LOOK QUIET
text: Even a galaxy full of life might not be a galaxy full of messages. For much of Earth's history, life was microbial. A planet can have active chemistry, ecosystems, and evolution without anybody building an antenna. Complex cells, large bodies, nervous systems, and technological societies are separate developments, not milestones that every living world is required to reach. Evolution does not aim at a radio telescope. It favors traits that affect reproduction in particular environments, with history and contingency shaping what becomes possible. We should also avoid the opposite mistake: treating Earth's sequence as the only imaginable route. Another biosphere might differ in ways we cannot predict. The honest position is narrower. Our one known example contains a long interval of life without human-style technology, and we do not know how typical that history is. This means two searches can have very different prospects. A search for atmospheric signs of biological activity could succeed in a universe where a search for deliberate interstellar transmissions remains unsuccessful. Life, intelligence, and detectable technology are related questions, not interchangeable words.

title: INTELLIGENCE DOES NOT GUARANTEE A TRANSMITTER
text: Consider the animals sharing our own world. Some solve problems, communicate, remember individuals, cooperate, and use tools. None of that automatically produces metallurgy, electricity, or an industrial supply chain. A technological civilization requires a particular combination of abilities, materials, environments, social arrangements, and accumulated knowledge. We do not know which ingredients are common elsewhere, or what different combinations might achieve. An ocean world could support sophisticated behavior while making familiar routes to fire and metalworking difficult. That is a possible constraint, not a proof that aquatic intelligence could never develop technology. Even a species with machines might not produce emissions that our instruments could recognize. Its communications could use unfamiliar channels, low power, narrow beams, or methods that leave little outward leakage. When we ask how many intelligent species exist, we are therefore asking something different from how many civilizations are visible to us. The galaxy might contain minds without transmitters, transmitters without strong leakage, and strong leakage that never crosses Earth's position. Each possibility changes what an empty observation can tell us.

title: THE EQUATION THAT ORGANIZES IGNORANCE
text: The Drake equation is useful here, provided we resist turning it into a fortune-telling device. It organizes factors such as star formation, planetary occurrence, the emergence of life, technological activity, and the length of time that activity remains detectable. Some factors can now be constrained by astronomy far better than they could when the equation was introduced. Others remain deeply uncertain. Multiply several guesses together and a neat-looking answer can conceal enormous uncertainty. A colorful graphic showing ten thousand civilizations is not a measurement simply because multiplication appears underneath it. Different reasonable assumptions can produce wildly different outcomes. The equation's strength is that it exposes where those assumptions enter. It also reminds us that a galaxy's total history is not the same as the number of civilizations detectable at the same time. A civilization could last a long time while producing a recognizable signal only briefly. Another might disappear while an automated beacon continued. What matters for a specific search is the duration and character of the detectable phenomenon, not just the lifespan of the people who made it.

title: THE TWO CLOCKS MUST OVERLAP
text: Imagine two islands where a lamp is switched on for a few minutes each century. Both islands can truthfully say that someone has used a lamp. That does not mean either island will see the other. In the galaxy, the clocks are much larger, and light takes time to cross the water. A signal arriving at Earth tonight was emitted in the past. Whether we detect it depends on its emission time, travel time, our observing schedule, and our sensitivity. There may also be no overlap between the eras in which two civilizations operate compatible technology. None of this establishes that civilizations are short-lived. It shows why the duration of detectable activity matters. We sometimes picture the galaxy's entire history as a crowded party whose guests must all be in the same room. In reality, the invitations could be separated by millions of years. If we search for active signals, timing matters directly. If we search for long-lived artifacts or environmental changes, we are asking a different question about how long a trace remains visible after its makers stop participating.

title: WHAT HAVE WE ACTUALLY LISTENED FOR?
text: Radio searches do not consist of pointing a dish upward and waiting for any conceivable alien voice. Researchers choose directions, frequency ranges, observing times, signal types, and thresholds for deciding what deserves attention. A narrowband signal can be interesting because concentrating energy into a very small frequency range may distinguish a transmitter from many natural sources. But the instrument must cover the relevant frequency at the relevant time with enough sensitivity. Researchers may also account for changes in apparent frequency caused by relative motion. Some surveys inspect many nearby stars. Others examine particular regions or different kinds of targets. These choices are scientifically motivated, but they are choices. A null result means that no qualifying signal was found within the tested conditions and the limits of the analysis. It does not mean no signal existed anywhere. This is how science gains ground without overclaiming: define a search, report its sensitivity and coverage, and let future work extend or revise it. A receiver that misses one kind of signal has not necessarily failed. It may have answered a precise, narrower question.

title: THE COSMIC HAYSTACK
text: A useful metaphor is a cosmic haystack with many dimensions. One dimension is position. Others include frequency, bandwidth, time, polarization, transmitter strength, and the behavior of a signal. How much of that haystack have we searched? Researchers have tried to quantify this question, but any fraction depends on how the haystack is defined. There is no universal percentage representing every possible technological phenomenon. A study of radio search completeness cannot automatically describe searches for infrared waste heat or optical pulses. The lesson is not a catchy tiny number. It is that the search space is large and our coverage is uneven. Imagine sampling a small patch of ocean and finding no fish. The result matters, but what it tells you depends on where you sampled, how deep, with what net, and what species you could catch. Likewise, repeated astronomical null results can rule out particular populations of sufficiently powerful transmitters under stated assumptions. They do not let us announce that the universe has been comprehensively checked. The absence becomes informative when we say exactly what would have been visible.

title: COULD THEY HEAR US?
text: Now reverse the telescope. How conspicuous is Earth? Our planet has emitted artificial radio signals for more than a century, but it has not illuminated the galaxy with a uniformly readable broadcast. Different emissions have different strengths, directions, frequencies, and schedules. Some powerful radar transmissions are highly directional. Ordinary leakage spreads and becomes difficult to distinguish at great distances, depending on the receiving instrument and the signal. The expanding region reached by our oldest emissions is also not a solid shell of intelligible television. A radio wave passing a location does not guarantee that anybody there can detect or decode it. Deliberate interstellar messages are a separate category, with their own limited targets and histories. There is no single, context-free distance beyond which Earth becomes invisible to every conceivable observer. Claims about detectability need assumptions about both transmitter and receiver. This should make us cautious about expecting another civilization to be obvious merely because it resembles us. We could be looking at a technological world whose most detectable activities rarely point our way, while its everyday life remains hidden in the noise.

title: WHEN A PROMISING SIGNAL IS NOT A DISCOVERY
text: Imagine that our observatory's strange signal returns. It has a sharp frequency structure and seems to move in an interesting way. The team does not announce a civilization. First, it asks whether the signal comes from the sky at all. Satellites, aircraft, ground equipment, electronics, and instrumental effects can create misleading patterns. Researchers compare observations on the target with observations away from it. They inspect the instrument and the local environment. They ask whether another observatory can reproduce the result, whether the position behaves like a distant source, and whether the signal persists under further analysis. An unexplained event is not automatically an extraterrestrial technology. A candidate can remain unresolved because the available data are insufficient, without becoming stronger evidence by remaining mysterious. Nor does rejecting a candidate make the search pointless. Learning how interference imitates a signal improves the next search. A convincing discovery would need a chain of evidence that survives serious efforts to find a mundane explanation. Our opening scene becomes extraordinary only when that chain holds. A dramatic first impression is the beginning of the investigation, not its conclusion.

title: MORE THAN RADIO
text: A technological signature does not have to be a greeting. Researchers discuss optical pulses, unusual atmospheric compounds, industrial effects, and infrared emissions associated with energy use. These are possibilities with different physical assumptions and practical limitations. An atmosphere can contain a molecule for natural reasons, and retrieving an atmospheric spectrum from a distant planet is difficult. An unusual light curve can arise from dust, stellar behavior, or other astrophysical causes. Infrared excess can also have ordinary explanations. The challenge resembles the one we faced in the Silurian Hypothesis: an unusual trace needs context, competing explanations, and independent checks. A hypothetical technology can be interesting to search for without being evidence that it exists. The value of multiple methods is that they ask different questions. A civilization that never sends a deliberate radio message could still alter its environment. Another might produce little detectable change by our methods. Broadening the search helps us avoid defining every possible civilization as a louder copy of twentieth-century Earth. It does not remove the need to establish what a proposed signature actually means.

title: THE CIVILIZATION THAT USES A STAR
text: One famous idea imagines a civilization collecting a substantial fraction of its star's energy. Popular illustrations often show a rigid shell surrounding the star. A more useful conceptual picture is a large population of orbiting collectors, although the engineering remains far beyond anything we can build. Such a system is a hypothesis, not an observed structure. Energy use would still involve thermodynamics: energy ultimately leaves in some form, often discussed as waste heat at infrared wavelengths. That gives astronomers a possible way to look for certain kinds of large-scale activity. But the temperature, geometry, fraction of starlight intercepted, and background environment affect what would be visible. A dusty natural system can also glow strongly in infrared. We cannot label every infrared-bright object a megastructure, and a null search for one design does not rule out all advanced societies. The deeper point is useful even without giant construction. A civilization's detectability may depend less on its desire to talk than on what its activities do to energy and matter. That shifts the search from listening for a sentence to examining a physical footprint.

title: WHY NOT JUST TRAVEL HERE?
text: At this point the original question returns with force. If messages are hard to catch, why has nobody simply arrived? Interstellar travel is not prohibited by known physics at speeds below light. It is, however, extraordinarily demanding. A probe must obtain energy, survive its environment, navigate, communicate, and possibly slow down at its destination. Dust and radiation matter. At high speeds, even small particles can become serious hazards. A human crew adds life support, health, reproduction, maintenance, and social continuity to the problem. None of these difficulties proves that a civilization with much more experience could never send anything. They do mean that a sketch of a starship is not an engineering demonstration. We should distinguish several claims: a journey is physically allowed, a machine can practically survive it, a society can afford it, and that society chooses to launch it repeatedly. Those are different steps. The Fermi question becomes more interesting when we admit both sides: the gulf between stars is real, yet the galaxy has existed for far longer than any human technological project.

title: A GALAXY CAN BE OLD ENOUGH
text: Consider a deliberately simplified model. Suppose probes or settlements can establish new launch sites, and those sites eventually send missions onward. Progress could occur through a chain of relatively local journeys rather than one ship crossing the galaxy in a single leap. In some models, even travel much slower than light can spread activity across large parts of the Milky Way on timescales short compared with its age. But the answer depends on assumptions about speed, waiting times, suitable destinations, survival, and whether new sites actually keep expanding. These models demonstrate possibilities. They do not show that expansion must happen. Stars also move, so the galaxy is not a fixed board of destinations. Researchers have explored how stellar motion and settlement behavior alter the result. We should therefore be suspicious of both simple extremes: nobody could ever cross between stars, or one civilization must inevitably occupy everything. The important tension survives between them. If long-lived, expanding technological populations are common, we need to explain why their effects are not more obvious. The strength of that expectation depends on the model behind it.

title: SPREADING IS NOT THE SAME AS FILLING
text: A civilization could reach multiple systems without occupying every suitable place. Some destinations might be unattractive. Some outposts might fail. Expansion could slow, stop, or change character. A population's priorities could shift over long periods, and the conditions for settlement may be more restrictive than a simple map assumes. This creates possibilities for patchy habitation and long gaps. It also reveals a limit in arguments about universal alien psychology. We cannot prove that all civilizations want to expand forever. We also cannot solve the whole problem by declaring that none of them would ever try. If there are many independent civilizations over billions of years, a claim about what every one of them chooses becomes a very strong claim. Diversity cuts both ways. It weakens assumptions of inevitable conquest, and it weakens explanations requiring perfect restraint everywhere. A scientifically useful model makes the behavior explicit and asks what observable distribution follows. An attractive story about wise societies staying home is still a story until we can connect it to evidence. Human history can suggest questions, but it is a poor universal rulebook for unknown minds.

title: WOULD WE RECOGNIZE A VISITOR'S TRACE?
text: Perhaps a visitor arrived long ago, left a small machine, and disappeared. Can we rule that out? Not comprehensively. Earth changes, artifacts can be small, and our inspection of the solar system is incomplete. But this possibility must not be turned into a claim that unusual rocks, human monuments, or ambiguous images are alien equipment. A proposed object needs material evidence, a reliable context, and tests that distinguish technology from natural formation or ordinary human activity. Durable artifacts on some airless surfaces might survive under conditions very different from Earth's, though impacts, radiation, and surface processes still matter. Researchers can discuss artifact searches without asserting that an artifact has been found. This is the direct bridge to our previous video. Preservation limits can hide traces, but they do not create positive evidence. A missing record cannot be filled with whichever civilization makes the most exciting picture. If an object were discovered, the strongest next step would be careful measurement and independent investigation. Until then, our illustrations of abandoned alien machines belong inside clearly marked imagination, not inside the evidence column.

title: THE GREAT FILTER
text: The Great Filter names another way to organize the puzzle. Between lifeless matter and a long-lived, widely detectable technological presence, there may be one or more exceptionally difficult transitions. Those transitions are called filters in the argument. The hard step might be the origin of life, the development of complex cells, the emergence of a technological species, or the persistence of technological activity. There could be several hard steps rather than one dramatic event. The framework is not a discovered physical barrier, and it does not locate a known deadline in humanity's future. Its emotional power comes from an uncertainty: have we already passed the hardest transitions, or are important ones still ahead? To answer, we would need evidence about how often transitions occur and what civilizations tend to do after them. Our single example cannot settle those rates. A filter is therefore a way of posing hypotheses, not a verdict that every society eventually destroys itself. The same quiet sky can be made to fit very different stories when the unknown probabilities are allowed to change. The job is to seek observations that separate those stories.

title: THE FILTER BEHIND US
text: Suppose a crucial biological transition is extraordinarily rare. Perhaps simple life is widespread but complex cells are uncommon. Or perhaps even the first self-sustaining evolutionary systems arise only under a narrow combination of conditions. Then the scarcity of detectable civilizations might have little to do with technological self-destruction. We could have passed a difficult bottleneck long before humans existed. This possibility is sometimes reassuring, but we should not mistake reassurance for evidence. Earth's history can constrain sequences and timescales; it does not provide a sample of thousands of independent worlds. Even discovering microbes elsewhere would require interpretation. An independent origin would inform the probability of life beginning, while a shared origin would answer a different question. Finding complex life would change another part of the discussion. No single discovery automatically locates every filter. What matters is which transition the discovery actually demonstrates. This is why astrobiology and the search for technology belong in the same conversation. The smallest organism in an extraterrestrial sample could tell us something about the silence of the sky that another century of speculative stories could not.

title: THE FILTER AHEAD OF US
text: Now consider the darker possibility: technological societies emerge fairly often, but their detectable phases tend to be brief. Conflict, ecological disruption, dangerous technologies, or other failures might limit persistence. These are serious subjects, yet the Fermi paradox does not give us a measured extinction rate for civilizations. We have not observed a population of alien societies rise and fall. We also need to distinguish the end of a broadcasting phase, the collapse of an institution, and the extinction of a species. A quieter civilization is not necessarily a dead one. A surviving society might change its infrastructure, reduce emissions, or become difficult to detect in ways unrelated to catastrophe. The future-filter idea can motivate responsible thinking about risks, but it cannot supply a date or a percentage for humanity's fate. Our choices still need to be evaluated using the evidence available for particular dangers. The sky is not a substitute for that work. An unresolved astronomical question should make us humble about our predictions, not give speculative doom the authority of an observation.

title: WHAT IF THEY SIMPLY DO NOT WANT TO TALK?
text: Another family of explanations concerns motivation. Perhaps civilizations are uninterested in strangers, communicate within private networks, or prefer observation to contact. The so-called zoo hypothesis imagines deliberate noninterference. The dark forest story imagines that revealing one's location is dangerous. Both can generate compelling fiction. Neither is an established description of the galaxy. A story requiring every independent civilization to follow the same rule, across enormous distances and times, faces a coordination problem. Even if secrecy were common, could every transmitter, machine, faction, and accident remain hidden? Conversely, we should not assume that advanced beings share our curiosity or our wish for public conversation. The honest boundary is that alien preferences are largely unknown. We can study the consequences of different assumptions, but we cannot read a motive directly from a null detection. Silence could reflect rarity, distance, timing, engineering, behavior, or our instruments. It is tempting to choose the most cinematic explanation and call the problem solved. A scientific explanation needs more than the ability to fit what we have not seen. It needs some way to earn support over its alternatives.

title: ARE WE EARLY TO THE PARTY?
text: What if the galaxy is quiet because many potential civilizations have not appeared yet? Some stars live far longer than the Sun, giving the future enormous possible stretches of time. But longevity does not guarantee habitability. Small, long-lived stars can present challenges involving activity, radiation, planetary atmospheres, and orbital conditions. We do not yet know how these factors combine to determine the long-term prospects for life and technology. Being early is therefore a hypothesis that depends on models of habitable environments, biological transitions, and the history of the universe. It is not a conclusion obtained just by noticing that some stars burn slowly. We should also separate the age of the whole universe from the ages and environments of individual planetary systems. Different worlds get different starting conditions and opportunities. The possibility is fascinating because it changes the emotional direction of the question. Instead of asking why the party has ended, we ask whether many guests have not arrived. But an appealing change of mood is not a measurement. The evidence still has to decide how much weight that possibility deserves.

title: WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY CHANGE THE ARGUMENT?
text: Imagine three future discoveries. First, researchers identify a convincing biological signal on another planet. They would still need to test nonbiological explanations, but a robust result could transform estimates of how widespread life is. Second, a narrowband transmission is repeatedly detected from a celestial source, independently verified, and shown to resist natural and human explanations. That would change the technological question far more directly. Third, a well-characterized artifact is found with properties and context that establish an origin beyond known human activity and natural formation. Each discovery would answer a different part of the problem. We should not promise that one spectrum, one strange image, or one exciting night will finish the investigation. Evidence can arrive gradually, through repeated measurements and competing analyses. Equally, null results can improve the argument when surveys become more sensitive or cover more of a clearly defined target population. Progress does not require a spectacular announcement every year. It requires a clearer account of what was tested, what would have been detected, and which possibilities remain open after the test.

title: HOW THE NEXT SEARCH GETS BETTER
text: The practical response to uncertainty is not to listen forever in exactly the same way. Researchers can expand sky coverage, observe across more frequencies, revisit targets, improve sensitivity, and develop methods for finding different signal behaviors. Optical and infrared searches can examine possibilities radio surveys do not test. Atmospheric studies can investigate biosignatures and proposed industrial signatures, with strong attention to false positives. Better catalogs help identify useful targets, while transparent analysis and independent checks make results easier to assess. No instrument eliminates every uncertainty. More data can reveal more interference as well as more astrophysics. But a systematic search turns a vague question into a collection of questions that can be answered. It also gives people something useful to do with curiosity. Instead of treating every unexplained light as a revelation, we can ask what observation would discriminate among explanations. Instead of treating every null result as failure, we can ask which part of the search space became better constrained. The night sky is not becoming less mysterious because we measure it. Its mysteries become more precise, and therefore more accessible to discovery.

title: OUR TELESCOPE GETS AN ANSWER
text: Return to the observatory from the beginning. The team checks its remarkable signal. In our imagined example, a second instrument does not confirm an astronomical source, and the pattern is eventually traced to interference. There is disappointment, of course. But the telescope has still done its job. It produced a candidate, the researchers tested it, and an attractive explanation lost to a better one. Now imagine the alternative: independent observatories keep finding the same celestial source, the evidence survives scrutiny, and the ordinary explanations fail under increasingly precise tests. The correct response would be neither instant certainty about alien intentions nor automatic dismissal. It would be a carefully communicated discovery with explicit limits. A signal might establish technology without telling us the senders' biology, politics, population, or present condition. If the source is distant, we would be learning about its past. Contact begins with evidence, not with a complete biography. This is why the standard matters before the discovery. The more extraordinary the possibility feels, the more valuable a patient method becomes. We want an answer we can trust after the excitement fades.

title: THE SILENCE WE CAN HONESTLY DESCRIBE
text: So, where is everybody? We do not know whether there is anybody else to find. We know that planets are common. We know that life and technology arose at least once. We know that our searches have not produced verified evidence of an extraterrestrial technological civilization, and that those searches cover only particular parts of a much larger set of possibilities. Rarity, timing, distance, behavior, and survival remain live questions rather than a solved list of causes. The Fermi paradox is powerful because it exposes how much can hide inside an assumption. A crowded galaxy is not guaranteed by a large number of stars. An empty galaxy is not established by an incomplete search. Between those claims lies a real scientific program: learn how worlds work, look for life, search for technology, and report what the evidence permits. Tonight, the chair beside the telescope is still empty. That is not proof that nobody will ever sit across from us. It is a reminder that we have only begun to ask the question in ways the universe can answer.
